stories.headline: Colorado voters to decide on constitutional 'right to natural gas' in November
stories.summary:
Colorado voters will consider a ballot measure in November that would enshrine a consumer right to purchase natural gas for home and business use in the state constitution. The Colorado Secretary of State's Office confirmed Thursday that backers of Initiative 177 submitted enough valid signatures — roughly 125,000, including thresholds in each of the state's 25 Senate districts — to qualify for the ballot.

The measure would prohibit state and local governments from banning or restricting natural gas sales and use, and would overturn any existing laws or regulations doing so. Because it amends the state constitution, Initiative 177 requires approval from 55% of voters to pass.

Advance Colorado, a conservative nonprofit that does not disclose its donors, crafted the measure and is funding the campaign. Initiative 177 will appear alongside at least seven other statewide measures, with the total possibly reaching 15.

stories.headline: Salmonella outbreak tied to jalapeños at Chipotle and Qdoba sickens 110 in Colorado
stories.summary:
Colorado public health officials have identified 110 cases of salmonella linked to a multistate outbreak involving more than 300 cases across at least 27 states, according to the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment and the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Investigators traced the source to jalapeño peppers grown in Mexico and distributed to U.S. restaurants.

In Colorado, the CDPHE said its investigation pointed to two chains serving the contaminated peppers: Chipotle and Qdoba. Both restaurants have since stopped serving the affected jalapeños after being notified of the outbreak, and state and federal authorities say there is no ongoing risk to consumers at those establishments.

Nationally, the outbreak has led to 36 hospitalizations, though no deaths have been reported. Salmonella symptoms — including diarrhea, stomach cramps and fever — typically appear six hours to six days after ingestion. State health officials warned that the number of Colorado cases could rise as laboratory testing continues.

stories.headline: Colorado River near Palisade drops to lowest flow in at least a decade, alarming water managers
stories.summary:
The Colorado River near Palisade briefly fell to just 42.9 cubic feet per second early Wednesday morning — its lowest recorded flow in at least 10 years — before rebounding to roughly 88 cfs by afternoon. A typical August flow at that gauge is around 1,200 cfs, making this year's readings starkly anomalous. The only comparable periods on record were August 2002 and April 2013.

Drought is the primary driver. Colorado's winter snowpack was the lowest since 1987 and began melting a month early due to a March heat wave. Headwaters regions are experiencing extreme to exceptional drought, the two most severe tiers tracked by the U.S. Drought Monitor, and the late-summer low flows typically seen in August are arriving a full month early.

The crisis is straining farmers, reservoir operators and endangered fish from the mountains to the Utah border. Dan Crabtree, superintendent of the Palisade Irrigation District, described conditions as "dire" and "record-setting," noting exposed rock shelves, drying side channels, rising water temperatures and algae buildup clogging irrigation infrastructure in the Grand Junction area.

stories.headline: Colorado relaunches e-bike rebate program offering $1,000 discounts to income-qualified residents
stories.summary:
The Colorado Energy Office announced Thursday the relaunch of a statewide e-bike rebate program that will provide $1,000 discounts to more than 2,800 income-qualified residents over the next year. The program is funded with $3 million from the state's Community Access Enterprise, which is supported by fees on residential online deliveries. Gov. Jared Polis joined Energy Office Director Will Toor at a Wheat Ridge bike shop to announce the initiative's return.

The program was previously offered in 2023 but ended in 2025 after its legislative appropriation was exhausted; nearly 8,000 Coloradans used it in that period. The relaunched version is limited to households earning 80% or less of their county's area median income — in metro Denver, that is up to $80,640 for an individual or $115,200 for a family of four.

In addition to the base $1,000 rebate, applicants can stack a $300 discount for cargo e-bikes and another $300 for adaptive e-bikes. Residents must enter a lottery beginning Aug. 24; if selected, they submit income and residency documentation. The program runs quarterly and is separate from an existing $225 point-of-sale tax credit available to all Colorado residents.

stories.headline: HDR closing Englewood office, moving 680 employees across metro Denver in major consolidation
stories.summary:
Engineering and architecture firm HDR is closing its Englewood office and simultaneously expanding its Greenwood Village presence while relocating approximately 500 downtown Denver employees to Block 162, a major office tower in the central business district. The consolidation affects roughly 680 employees across the metro area.

The moves represent one of the more significant corporate real estate shifts in the Denver metro in recent months, reshaping HDR's local footprint across multiple submarkets. HDR is a global firm with a substantial Colorado presence in infrastructure, transportation and water project work.

The relocation to Block 162 continues a pattern of companies consolidating into newer, higher-quality downtown office space, a trend that has provided some lift to Denver's central business district even as overall office vacancy remains elevated.

stories.headline: Denver metro home sales cool in July as mortgage rates climb toward 6.8%
stories.summary:
Metro Denver home closings fell 11.8% in July to 3,667, down from 4,158 in June and off 5.7% compared to a year earlier, according to the Denver Metro Association of Realtors' monthly report. The pullback was driven partly by seasonal factors as families sought housing stability ahead of the school year, but rising 30-year mortgage rates — climbing from roughly 6.3% in June to near 6.8% by month's end — also weighed on demand.

The median price of a single-family home that closed in July was $660,000, down 2.2% from June's $675,000 but 1.5% above the year-ago figure. Condos and townhomes fared worse, with median sold prices falling 2.6% to $380,000 on both a monthly and annual basis; condos are taking a median of 40 days to sell compared to 17 days for single-family homes.

Active inventory stood at 13,115 listings at month's end, up slightly from June but well below the July historical average of 15,347. A separate Redfin analysis found affordability for starter homes in Denver improving for the eighth consecutive month, with roughly 68% of starter homes accessible to a household earning the city's median income of $116,323.

stories.headline: Sundance Film Festival's Colorado move sparks new cultural partnerships, including Red Rocks screening
stories.summary:
Denver Film and the Sundance Film Festival partnered for a special 20th anniversary screening of "Little Miss Sunshine" at Red Rocks Amphitheatre, offering an early glimpse of the collaborations organizers say will become more frequent now that Sundance has relocated to Colorado. The event at the iconic Morrison venue drew attention to the broader cultural and economic opportunities the festival's move is expected to create for the state's film and arts community.

Sundance's relocation from Park City, Utah, to Colorado was one of the most closely watched decisions in the independent film world, and local organizations are now working to build institutional ties with the festival. Denver Film, which operates the annual Denver Film Festival, has positioned itself as a natural partner given its existing infrastructure and venue relationships.

The partnership signals that Colorado's arts community intends to integrate Sundance into the state's cultural calendar rather than treat it as a standalone event, with Red Rocks emerging as a potential marquee venue for future festival programming.

stories.headline: Colorado universities partner with ChatGPT as student AI resisters push back on campus adoption
stories.summary:
The University of Colorado and Colorado State University have each struck deals to deploy institution-specific versions of ChatGPT for students and faculty, with CU's $2 million OpenAI partnership reaching more than 28,000 users at the Boulder campus by March. University administrators argue the partnerships provide equitable, secure access to tools students are already using and prepare graduates for AI-integrated workplaces.

A growing contingent of students is pushing back. CU Boulder graduate researcher Mirakle Wright, who is studying AI-avoidant students, found that participants cited environmental concerns over the technology's water use, data privacy issues, objections to AI scraping existing creative work, and fears of self-described cognitive decline. Most of her subjects said they believe AI has no place in higher education.

The tension reflects a wider national debate playing out with particular intensity at Colorado's flagship institutions, where administrative enthusiasm for AI partnerships is colliding with student and faculty concerns about academic integrity, intellectual development and the role of technology in learning.

stories.headline: Anythink Libraries to open Nature Library on 15 acres in Thornton this weekend
stories.summary:
Anythink Libraries will open its new Nature Library location in Thornton on Saturday, Aug. 8, with a free community celebration from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. The 33,000-square-foot facility sits on 15 acres adjacent to the 140-acre Aylor Open Lands at 6811 E. 136th Ave. and features interactive nature labs, gardens, a one-mile trail loop, a café and a sunroom.

The opening event will include live performances, storytimes, guided nature walks, interactive art experiences and family activities. The location is designed to blend library programming with outdoor and environmental education, offering hands-on experiences for visitors of all ages.

The Nature Library represents an expansion of the Anythink system, which serves the Rangeview Library District in the northern Denver suburbs. Officials describe it as one of Colorado's newest cultural destinations.

stories.headline: Broncos get positive injury news on Nik Bonitto, Courtland Sutton at training camp
stories.summary:
Denver Broncos outside linebacker Nik Bonitto, who had missed practice earlier in the week with a minor injury, returned to limited work Thursday, taking walk-through reps as the team practiced without pads. Head coach Sean Payton indicated the $106 million All-Pro pass rusher is progressing well and is not considered a significant concern.

Wide receiver Courtland Sutton missed a third consecutive practice day but participated in walk-through reps, with both Sutton and Payton emphasizing the absence reflects a deliberate workload management plan rather than injury. Sutton, who turns 30 this season, said the team presented him with Catapult tracking data supporting a lighter camp load to preserve his health for the full regular season.

Wide receiver Jaylen Waddle is dealing with a muscle strain but is expected back in four to five days, Payton said. In the backfield, J.K. Dobbins, RJ Harvey and rookie Jonah Coleman are emerging as the team's top three running backs, with competition ongoing for third-down and passing-game roles.

stories.headline: Cale Makar extension negotiations complicated by NHL salary explosion and CBA deadline
stories.summary:
Colorado Avalanche defenseman Cale Makar has yet to sign an extension, and the NHL landscape has shifted dramatically since general manager Joe Sakic said in June that real negotiations would begin in mid-July. A wave of record-setting contracts — including Leo Carlsson's five-year, $90 million deal and Macklin Celebrini's five-year, $94 million extension with San Jose — has reset expectations for elite players leaguewide.

A critical procedural deadline adds urgency for the Avalanche: teams can only sign their own players to eight-year extensions until around Sept. 16, when NHL teams are expected to report to training camp and when the expiring collective bargaining agreement would reduce maximum contract term to seven years. An eighth year on a Makar deal would cover his age-36 season, potentially allowing a lower salary in that final year to reduce the overall cap hit.

Makar's next contract is set to begin in the 2027-28 season, the same year deals for Quinn Hughes and Nikita Kucherov are also expected to kick in, meaning the market for elite defensemen will be shaped by multiple high-profile negotiations happening simultaneously. Avalanche fans and league observers are watching closely, with Makar widely considered the best defenseman in the sport.

stories.headline: Rockies front office signals possible earlier competitive window after measured trade deadline
stories.summary:
Colorado Rockies general manager Paul DePodesta's comments following this week's trade deadline are prompting reassessment of the new front office's timeline. Rather than selling broadly, the Rockies moved only pitcher Antonio Senzatela among impending free agents and instead traded players with multiple years of team control — including outfielder Brenton Doyle and pitchers Seth Halvorsen and Victor Vodnik — suggesting the front office sees near-term upside in its current roster.

DePodesta told reporters the Rockies set firm asking prices for all players and declined deals that didn't meet that threshold. He also pointed to the team's June offensive performance — ranking among the best in baseball that month — as evidence the foundation of something competitive may already be in place, with corner outfielder Michael Moniak and starting pitcher Kyle Freeland under contract through at least 2028.

Analysts at Purple Row note the moves are incongruous with a straightforward rebuild targeting a 2029 or later contention window, raising the possibility the Rockies believe they can be a wildcard contender within two to three seasons. The coming months will test whether the front office's optimism about its in-house talent is vindicated or reflects an overly aggressive reading of a small sample.

topStory.headline: Trump-Backed Tennessee Congressman Ogles Loses Primary to Establishment-Backed Hatcher
topStory.summary:
Republican Rep. Andy Ogles of Tennessee lost his bid for reelection Thursday, defeated in the GOP primary for the redrawn 5th Congressional District by Charlie Hatcher, a former state agriculture commissioner and dairy farmer. Hatcher secured the Republican nomination despite a last-minute "tele-rally" appearance by President Trump on Ogles' behalf, and will face Democrat Chaz Molder, the mayor of Columbia, in the November general election.

Hatcher built his winning coalition around prominent establishment Republican figures, drawing endorsements from outgoing Gov. Bill Lee, former Gov. Bill Haslam, and former Trump cabinet member Sonny Perdue. Though Trump had backed Ogles, Hatcher closely aligned himself with the president throughout his campaign, describing Trump on his website as "the most impactful president of our lifetime." Hatcher narrowly defeated Ogles even in Maury County, Ogles' home turf.

Ogles had accumulated significant political baggage since winning his seat in 2022. He faced scrutiny for misrepresenting his professional background, filing incorrect and late campaign finance disclosures, making a disputed $230,000 personal loan to his own campaign, and publicly stating that "Muslims don't belong in American society." A federal investigation stemming from the financial disclosures was largely abandoned earlier this year, but the controversies contributed to eroding his standing with voters.

The race also unfolded against a backdrop of aggressive Republican redistricting in Tennessee. The state legislature redrew the 5th District map earlier this year, a move designed to bolster national GOP midterm efforts by splitting Memphis across multiple districts. The new district now stretches from parts of Williamson and Maury counties northwest through rural West Tennessee and down the Mississippi River into Memphis, significantly changing the electorate Ogles had originally represented.

With the Republican nomination secured, Hatcher is favored to win the deeply red district in November, though Molder enters the general election with more than $2.5 million in reserves. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee had previously committed to supporting Molder's campaign when he was running in the old, more competitive district, though the redrawn boundaries have made a Democratic victory considerably more difficult.
